newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany, France look to make up at Friday summit.
newsitem.headline: Germany, France look to make up at Friday summit.

text.p: Germany and France, now ready to agree on a Maastricht jobs deal, hope to find one voice on Europe's planned stability pact on Friday to ensure a successful European Union summit next week, officials said.

The stability pact, a code of fiscal discipline due to give Europe's monetary union (EMU) a heavy German accent, will top the agenda at the six-monthly consultation of the EU's core alliance in the western French city of Poitiers.

But Chancellor Helmut Kohl, suddenly no longer Europe's undisputed giant after the French election and his bungled Bundesbank gold grab, will have to let more Gallic tones join the chorus to ensure his dream project EMU stays on track.

The trick will be to find a formula that gives France some concession on fighting unemployment but will not cost German taxpayers more money. Commentator Josef Joffe remarked in Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung this meant a weak euro or a rise in "the growing hypocrisy quotient in Europe".

Both German and French officials stressed they wanted a harmonious meeting, which will be Kohl's first with the new duo of Gaullist President Jacques Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.
"I'm sure we'll agree with France on the stability pact, so I think we don't have to be so worried about that," said Werner Hoyer, Bonn's chief Maastricht reforms negotiator.
"Since so many things are unclear on the international scene, the French-German relationship is more important than ever," a French official said.

Bowing to the EU's new leftward lean following the British and French elections, Bonn agreed on Wednesday to add a jobs chapter to the revised Maastricht treaty due to be approved at the EU summit in Amsterdam next week.
German officials said they were still considering an extra jobs resolution to be added to the stability pact, which France says it cannot sign in its present form.

The officials gave no details but one source said an idea already proposed and rejected would allow an overshoot on the Maastricht three percent deficit-to-GDP criteria, the target the stability pact was meant to defend, if that extra borrowing was used to boost employment. That approach was too Keynesian for Kohl's centre-right government.
There would have to be some substance in the resolution, another official said, adding Jospin could not be given only a "fig-leaf resolution" to take back to Paris.

Both EU Commission President Jacques Santer and Prime Minister Wim Kok of the Netherlands, the current EU president, have been visiting EU states in a frantic search for a solution before Monday's Amsterdam summit.

The Jospin government stunned Bonn on Monday by asking for a delay to study the stability pact, which French leftists see as a monetary straitjacket that runs counter to the greater political influence they want to see on EU policy.
French officials said the new government was in a stronger bargaining position vis-a-vis Germany, which one said "was not in a position to pound its fist on the table".
But Pierre Lellouche, an adviser to Chirac and member of parliament for the defeated Gaullist party, said France must not press its case so far that it endangers EMU.

"Don't forget a big majority of the German public doesn't want a single currency, so if we give the impression of having doubts, it won't happen," he told LCI television. "Let's be careful not to play too much this balancing act between election promises and France's international commitments."
The German business daily Handelsblatt said the bilateral summit had to find a compromise if Europe was to remain a major player in the world economy.

"Kohl would do well at the German-French summit to get rid of the remaining irritations over French policy with Chirac and Jospin," it wrote. "Paris and Bonn must have an interest in seeing that Europe is not pushed aside in the world economy.
"Globalisation will in the end force the EU to enter the race for world markets with a common currency."
